narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 65% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year class rank also worked against you, though to a lesser degree; you finished in the third decile compared with an average around the sixth decile for admitted students. These two indicators of how you performed relative to your classmates carried more weight than any other information.

Your LSAT score of 34 worked in the opposite direction. It was slightly below the 37-point average of accepted students, yet it still nudged the model gently toward a higher chance of passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to offset the impact of your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender, race, family income, undergraduate GPA, or plans to attend full-time; none of those played a role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most influenced this decision. (218 words)
